# How the investigation developed {#sec-storyline}

The work did not proceed as a straight line from question to answer. It moved through seven phases, and at several points a
confident statement was later corrected. The corrections are part of the result, because they show which beliefs the
evidence supports and which it does not. Throughout, "official benchmark images" means the images reconstructed by the
benchmark organisers from simulated phantoms (@sec-identifiability); no scanner or patient data are involved.

## 1. A toy model, and a lesson about our own tests

The first question was general: what limits material estimation from spectral CT, the estimator or the measurements? In a
small simulated model with water, iodine and calcium (@sec-mismatch) the answer separated into a structural part (rank,
which no estimator can beat) and an empirical part (conditioning, which differs between designs).

The same study produced two corrected beliefs. First, a comparison seemed to show that photon counting costs noise.
[We first reported a 2.7-fold noise penalty for photon counting, but that ratio compared a three-material fit with a
two-material fit; at equal basis size the idealised photon-counting design is about 2.5 times better at most.]{#clm-0122 .claim}
Second, our pre-registered test for bias from a wrong spectrum was itself flawed. [We first read that test as showing dual-kVp
estimation to be insensitive to spectral mismatch; successive reviews replaced this reading with the current one, that every
condition tested was biased, in one case only marginally (the per-ray bias was below the noise floor and became detectable
only by pooling rays), and that our detection statistic had been hiding it.]{#clm-0123 .claim}
That current reading is a noise-free calculation in a toy model and has itself not been independently reviewed.

## 2. The benchmark, and an optimistic first picture

We then moved to a public benchmark of dual-energy phantoms with three materials (@sec-theory). The linear algebra suggested
a hopeful picture. [We recorded exact recovery as the expected route: with the data noiseless and the model shared, adding the
constraint that fractions sum to one was expected to make the problem uniquely solvable, and on synthetic data we generated
with the same linear model, recovery was exact to numerical precision.]{#clm-0124 .claim} A related belief held that the
requirement that fractions be nonnegative would bound the family of indistinguishable solutions. [We first believed that
nonnegativity bounds the ambiguity, from an example whose decoy was physically unreachable; a recomputation found an exact
nonnegative decoy 19.7 cm away in path-length space.]{#clm-0125 .claim}

## 3. Reality check

On the official benchmark images (three kit cases at first, later 100 validation cases) the picture reversed
(@sec-identifiability). The benchmark data are noise-free, but the linear model we had inverted is not the model that
generated them, and the near-singular matrix magnified that mismatch. [On three official benchmark images the unclipped
sum-to-one estimator was worse than predicting zero (error 1.555 against 0.447), and on 100 validation cases it was about
3.4 times worse (1.508 against 0.446).]{#clm-0126 .claim} The earlier exact-recovery result had been an inverse crime
that we had not labelled as one. Claims about which classical estimator wins also failed to transfer. [We first reported that
a simplex-projected estimator looked best, but that held only on synthetic images, where clipping bounded the outliers of the
exact estimator; on the benchmark images the unconstrained estimator beat it, and on 100 validation cases total-variation
regularisation was the best classical method, although its weight landed on the largest value tried, so a better classical
result may lie beyond the grid (@sec-labelfree).]{#clm-0127 .claim}

## 4. The hypothesis, and a negative control by design

The scientific question was whether a network could learn the materials from measurement consistency alone. Theory said it could
not: a one-dimensional family of wrong answers fits the data exactly (@sec-theory). Two recent papers that looked like
precedents turned out to address easier problems (@sec-labelfree). [We therefore planned the label-free network as a negative
control from the start, whose purpose was to reveal which member of the ambiguous family the network's biases choose.]{#clm-0128 .claim}
An early toy-scale ladder confirmed the pattern, with one unexplained result: the label-free error was stable across seeds
while its consistency loss was not. Its test of whether a soft sum penalty helps was badly designed by us (a soft penalty at an
arbitrary weight against the hard constraint the theory concerned), so that half of the ladder was inconclusive. We also
checked that our tools were not the culprit (@sec-trust). [The differentiable forward model matches the official generator to
float32 rounding, and an earlier general model agrees with an independent simulator to about 0.5-1% with the simulator's own
spectrum (a check of the adapter and geometry, since both share the transport equation, not an independent validation) and
2-3% with ours.]{#clm-0129 .claim}

## 5. At scale: fit is not accuracy

On the full benchmark the prediction held (@sec-labelfree). [A supervised network reduced the validation error to about 0.02
while a label-free network fitted the measurements better and left the materials badly wrong, at about 0.30.]{#clm-0130 .claim}
Refinement, single added priors and alternative output forms did not change this in the settings tried (mostly single seeds
and two weights per prior), with one unexplained run as the exception. Diagnostics found collapses to constant outputs, with a
cause that was not isolated.

## 6. Where the question moved

[The question shifted from which loss function could remove the ambiguity to what additional information would resolve it,
because no loss tried, at the weights and seeds studied, avoided inheriting its answer from the model's implicit biases; we
hypothesise that information, not the loss, is missing.]{#clm-0056 .claim} Analysis of the null direction, of which simple
priors can discriminate, and of the information content of different acquisitions (@sec-information) points to knowledge about
calcification and the sum of the fractions, and to prior structure that breaks the fat-versus-gland symmetry. That is a
hypothesis resting on preliminary, single-ray and training-case analyses.

## 7. The first test of the information hypothesis

A staged plan separates information from optimisation. Its first stage, deterministic profiles around the truth, is done. Its
second stage was a bounded pilot of converged per-case solves on three validation cases, approved by the project owner and now
complete. [In the pilot, supplying the tissue sum from the truth and fixing calcification at zero reduced the clipped material
error to a few per cent, but only one of the three cases met the convergence rule, the unclipped error remained 0.21 to
0.44, the arm's own positive control failed on all three cases, no start without oracle information was shown to be
converged and recovered, and the arms that dropped the sum failed for modelling and numerical reasons.]{#clm-0131 .claim} So the pilot has not yet
tested the hypothesis in the label-free sense: its oracle arms measure information limits with the sum known. Whether to
proceed to network priors is left to the project owner (@sec-open).

## How belief changed

| Earlier belief | What changed it | Current reading |
|---|---|---|
| A dual-kVp estimator is not detectably biased by a wrong spectrum | A defective test; a corrected statistic | Every condition tested was biased; one case is marginal per ray and detectable only when rays are pooled (toy model, noise-free calculation; the later amendment is unreviewed) |
| Photon counting costs more noise | A comparison that confounded design with basis size | About 2.5 times better at most, idealised |
| Nonnegativity bounds the ambiguity | A reachable, nonnegative decoy at 19.7 cm | It does not bound it |
| Sum-to-one gives exact recovery | Official benchmark images; linear-model misfit amplified by conditioning | Unique on paper; unusable in the image-domain inversion tested |
| Simplex is the best classical choice | Benchmark-image comparison; its win is clipping | Unconstrained beats simplex on three images; total-variation regularisation is best of the classical methods on 100 cases, at the edge of its weight grid |
| A label-free physics loss might recover the materials (the initial aim, reframed before the first controlled experiment as a negative control) | Negative control at scale | Not by itself in the settings tried |
| (Current hypothesis) Information, not the loss, is missing | Null-direction, prior and acquisition analyses | Untested in practice; the first pilot supplied the sum from the truth and so does not decide it |
| (Current hypothesis) Calcification and sum knowledge would resolve the split | Single-ray bounds; the pilot | Supported only as an information limit with the sum known; sum-free and label-free versions untested |

: Beliefs that were revised, and why. The last two rows are current hypotheses, not revisions. {#tbl-belief}

[Six earlier beliefs were revised: dual-kVp insensitivity to spectral mismatch, a photon-counting noise penalty, the
nonnegativity bound, exact recovery with the sum constraint, simplex as the best classical choice, and the label-free
physics loss as a route to the materials.]{#clm-0065 .claim}

[Independent review overturned or narrowed earlier findings at least seven times, among them the recoverability claim for
the sum constraint, the nonnegativity bound, the insensitivity of dual-kVp estimation to spectral mismatch and a simulator
comparison.]{#clm-0057 .claim} [The project's rule that a superseding finding needs its own independent review has not
been met for the most recent corrections: no review is recorded for the corrections of the sum-constraint, nonnegativity
and classical-ranking claims or the simulator comparison, and the null-direction and pilot findings await re-review.]{#clm-0066 .claim}
That is one reason the current findings are labelled preliminary.
